n: Micah came from Moresheth, a farming town in Judah’s foothills. He prophesied about 740–700 BC, the same era as Isaiah, to both capitals: Samaria in the north and Jerusalem in the south.

f.g: His name means “Who is like Jehovah?” — a question echoed in Micah 7:18.
From Moresheth-gath, about 25 miles (40 km) southwest of Jerusalem.

n: Like a court summons, Micah calls all people and the whole earth to hear, with the Lord Himself as witness from His heavenly temple.
The Lord is pictured stepping out of heaven and striding across the earth’s heights. When God comes to judge, creation reacts.

f.w: the LORD cometh forth out of his place

f.g: Mountain heights — and also the hilltop shrines where idols were worshiped.

n: Mountains melt like wax near fire and valleys split open like water rushing down a slope. No power can stand before God.

f.w: the mountains shall be molten under him

n: Why does He come? Because of Israel’s sins. The capitals themselves, Samaria and Jerusalem, have become the centers of corruption.

f.g: Here the northern kingdom, Israel.
Shrines for false worship; Micah says Jerusalem itself has become one.

n: Samaria will be reduced to a heap of rubble, fit only for planting vines. Its stones will tumble down the hillside. Assyria destroyed it in 722 BC.

f.g: Uncover, lay bare.

n: Samaria’s idols will be smashed. Their wealth, gained through spiritual “prostitution” (unfaithfulness to God), will be carried off as plunder to pay other idolaters.

f.g: Wages — here, the gifts given at pagan shrines.

n: Micah grieves openly. He goes barefoot and stripped like a mourner or captive, crying like jackals and ostriches in the desert.

f.g: Jackals.
Ostriches, known for their mournful cries.

n: Samaria’s “wound” cannot be healed — and it is spreading to Judah, right up to Jerusalem’s gate. Assyria’s King Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC.

f.w: he is come unto the gate of my people

n: Micah begins a lament full of wordplays on town names along the invasion route. “Tell it not in Gath” echoes David’s lament for Saul. In Beth-aphrah (“house of dust”), roll in the dust.

f.w: Declare ye it not at Gath

f.g: Beth-le-aphrah means “house of dust.”

n: Shaphir (“beautiful”) will go into exile in shameful nakedness. Zaanan (sounds like “come out”) will not come out. Beth-ezel’s mourning means it can offer no support.

f.g: “Beautiful town” — its beauty becomes shame.
Sounds like Hebrew for “go out”; its people dare not go out.
Perhaps “house of nearness/support.”

n: Maroth (“bitterness”) hoped for good, but disaster from the Lord reached Jerusalem’s gate.

f.g: Means “bitterness.”

n: Lachish, Judah’s great fortress city, is told to harness horses to flee. It was where Israel’s sins first took root in Judah — perhaps by trusting chariots instead of God.

f.g: Its name sounds like rekesh, “steed.” Sennacherib’s siege of Lachish is pictured in famous Assyrian wall carvings.

n: Judah will give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath, Micah’s hometown, as it is lost. Achzib (“deceit”) will prove deceptive to Israel’s kings.

f.g: Farewell gifts or dowry — like giving away a daughter.
Sounds like akhzav, “deceptive brook” — a stream that dries up.

n: Mareshah (“possession”) will get a new possessor — a conqueror. Israel’s glory (its nobles) will hide in the caves of Adullam, where David once fled.

f.g: A conqueror who takes possession.

n: Shave your heads in grief, as bald as a vulture, for your beloved children are going into exile.

f.g: Cut off your hair.
Probably a vulture, whose head is bare.
